messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mika grew up in a house where danger announced itself before anyone spoke. His stepfather would come in from the garage smelling of singed metal and burnt oil, and Mika learned as a boy that the odor meant he should go still, watchful, ready for the blow or the grabbing hand. The abuse was physical and unpredictable, often set off when his stepfather had been drinking and tinkering with tools, and what stayed with Mika most was not a neat sequence but fragments: the smell, a shirt front close to his face, the heat of rage in his own body, the certainty that no one was coming to stop it. Even now, when he tries to explain what happened, he loses the thread and trails off, jaw tight, as if the story breaks apart under him.

He became a detective decades later, a job that had seemed to fit the version of himself that could stay hard, observant, and hard to surprise. But the work also keeps putting him near the kinds of cues that catch him off guard. In interviews with injured children or vulnerable adults, it is often the face of someone who resembles the child he once was that hits him first. At fire scenes or in shabby apartments with scorched pans, the burnt smell can pull the whole memory back without warning. The reaction is immediate and bodily: a rush in his chest, clenched muscles, a sense that he has to move or strike. When that happens, he does not think of it as remembering; it feels as if the past has broken into the room.

Those moments have shaped the habits of his adult life. On cases where a victim’s age, expression, or frightened posture resembles his younger self, Mika shortens the interaction or hands it to a colleague when he can. He keeps his distance from people generally outside work, telling himself it is easier that way, and since his divorce he has let that harden into a routine of going home alone and staying there. He is oddly particular about clothes, avoiding shirts and jackets that resemble what he remembers from that house, as if certain cuts or fabrics could make him feel too close to that boy again. He calls it being practical, but the logic is simple to him: if a smell, a face, or even a feeling of warmth and ease can open the trapdoor, then he has to narrow his world.

The effort to wall things off has not brought relief. When Mika feels a memory rising, he detaches from it, goes blank on purpose, pushes it away before it can fully form. Yet this seems to leave the past more jagged rather than less. Because he never stays with it long enough to put it into words, the memory remains in flashes that arrive with greater force, and when it does break through he is flooded with rage. The anger frightens him almost as much as the memory itself. He has come to see these reactions as proof that there is something fundamentally defective in him—that the abuse happened because of the kind of person he was, weak or marked somehow, and that the fact he still reacts this way means he is a lousy coper.

That belief has deepened over time because his body never stands down. He sleeps lightly and badly, lying awake as if some part of him still has to listen for footsteps in the hall. At work and in public he scans constantly, tracking voices, movements, exits. This permanent state of guard leaves him feeling that the world’s basic rules were shattered long ago, that safety is a story other people tell themselves. And when he notices how keyed up he is over something as small as a burnt smell from the break-room toaster, he reads it as more evidence of personal failure, not injury.

The loop has tightened in ways he can now see but not interrupt. The more he avoids certain people, clothes, and situations, the more unfamiliar ordinary contact feels, and even positive emotions have become confusing to him. A moment of warmth with a colleague, a brief sense of comfort, can feel dangerous in its own right, as if letting down his guard would invite harm; he becomes wary of the very states that might have connected him to others. That narrowing of his life leaves him alone with the fragments, and alone they return more abruptly. The repeated jolts of memory make him more watchful; the watchfulness makes burnt smells, familiar faces, and even good moments stand out as possible threats; and each new reaction seems to confirm his view that something is wrong with him at the core.

What finally brought Mika to treatment was an interview with a teenage assault victim who looked enough like him at that age that he felt himself go hot and lose the room. He had to leave, and afterward he sat in his car shaking, furious, and unable to give a clear account of why. For the first time, he worried his way of managing this was costing him the work he has built his life around. He says he wants help sleeping and “getting a handle on it,” but what frightens him most is the possibility that the past has fixed him permanently, and what he barely allows himself to hope is that these reactions might make sense without meaning he is ruined.
